Figure 2 shows the final experimental set up that is capable of drying laboratory made paper hand sheets under variety of drying conditions and collect instantaneous dying characteristics data. The experimental setup used in this study was custom machined by PSC Inc. (a Litzer company), using process and conceptual designs provided by the authors. Figure 3 shows the process and instrumentation diagram for the laboratory scale experimental drying setup with all the necessary instrumentation for measuring the various drying process variables including temperature, flow, humidity, pressure and load and continuous data acquisition and monitoring. In addition to the Laminar Flow Element (LFE) at the air inlet for 11 DE-EE0009395 accurate measurement of airflow, one of the key measurements are the precise water vapor concentration at the inlet and outlet of the drying tunnel using a Tunable Diode Laser Absorption Spectroscopy (TDLAS). A Tunable Diode Laser Absorption Spectroscopy (TDLAS) sensor is a high-precision sensor that is capable of accurately measuring the concentrations of water vapor in the air based on the absorption of IR energy by the water molecules in the air. The sample sled for holding the 8” x 8” paper sample is shown in Figure 4. Figure 3: Process and Instrumentation diagram of the drying system Figure 4: Sample sled The flow rate of the air supplied by the fan is measured using a high-precision flow measurement device, namely the Laminar Flow Element (LFE). The supply air stream is heated with an in-line heater controlled to a constant air temperature set point. The supply air to the dryer is then controlled using manual dampers with bypass capability allowing for safe loading and unloading of the sample. The air stream then converges into a 0.2 meter x 0.1 meter (0.2 m x 0.1 m) rectangular duct with a perforated plate at the end to ensure adequate mixing of the air. Then, it enters the Tunnel-Chamber System’s inner rectangular channel. 12 DE-EE0009395 The chambers in the tunnel have a total of six pneumatically controlled pistons/cylinders that have various modules attached to them for specific experimentation. The tunnel system consists of 4 chambers: • Chamber 0: Measurement chamber, also the sample loading and unloading chamber. The Teflon sample holder (Figure 4), mounted on a linear actuator, travels between the chambers. • Chamber 1 and 3: Both chambers are conduction enabled zones with a heated platen that can come in contact with the sheet. Chamber 1 has a hotplate attached to the bottom pneumatic cylinder and a perforated support with dryer fabric attached to the top cylinder. Chamber 3 has the hotplate on the top and dryer fabric on the bottom cylinder. • Chamber 2: This chamber is used for auxiliary energy inputs including Radio Frequency (RF) and Ultrasonic sound (US) applications. Further details on the experimental system and data collection and analysis are also provided in three published papers [Sampath et al [2025, 2024a, 2024b].
